newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Peacekeepers to oversee Bangui return to barracks.
newsitem.headline: Peacekeepers to oversee Bangui return to barracks.

text.p: The Central African Republic's government invited all disaffected soldiers to return to barracks from Tuesday after three mutinies in a year and urged loyalist soldiers to welcome them back.
Junior Defence Minister General Didas Ndayen, in a statement on state radio on Monday, said that African peacekeepers would accompany the mutineers back to their respective barracks by May 16.

A first group of several hundred former mutineers returned to Kassai Barracks in the capital Bangui on April 18 under a new commander as part of a process of national reconciliation brokered by Mali's former military leader Amadou Toumani Toure.

An estimated 100 of the 700 mutineers remain in Bangui's southern Petevo suburb, one of their strongholds during the revolts, which began over pay and conditions but turned into a campaign to oust President Ange-Felix Patasse, a northern civilian who won election in 1993.
Ndayen urged Patasse loyalists, principally in the presidential guard, to show a spirit of "comradeship in arms" and reserve "a good welcome" for the returnees.

The first mutinies were in April and May 1996. The third, which began on November 15, degenerated into ethnic bloodshed. French troops, in the country under a defence pact, restored order and handed over to African peacekeepers.

Toumani Toure brokered a January 25 peace plan after clashes between mutineers and French troops but mutual suspicion between the southern mutineers and Patasse loyalists persisted. Mutineers and peacekeepers clashed in March.
The peacekeepers include soldiers from Burkina Faso, Chad, Gabon, Mali, Senegal and Togo.
The mutineers are principally from the southern Yakoma tribe of former military leader Andre Kolingba. Estimates of the number of people killed in the mutinies range from scores to several hundred.
